outcomes.term: Why are intangible assets not in the balance sheet?

outcome.referenceAnswer: Intangible assets are non-physical resources — brands, patents, customer relationships — that are expected to generate future economic benefit. Most never appear on the balance sheet because of verifiability: when a company builds an intangible itself, there is no market transaction to establish what it is worth, so any booked amount would be an unverifiable management estimate. Accounting rules therefore require the costs of internally generated intangibles to be expensed as incurred rather than capitalized. And because the balance sheet must be auditable — with conservatism favoring understating assets over overstating them — those unverifiable internal intangibles stay off the books. The exception proves the rule: acquired intangibles like brands, technology, and goodwill do appear, because the arm's-length purchase price gives auditors an objective, verifiable value they can tie back to acquisition documents. So intangibles are excluded not because they lack value, but because accounting only recognizes value it can verify: what you built yourself stays off, what you bought and can evidence goes on.

probes.text: Well, I think it's basically because intangible assets are, you know, hard to put a number on. Like brands and reputation and things like that. Accounting has all these rules and conventions, and I guess intangible assets just don't really fit the way the system thinks about things. There are probably standards that say when you can and can't include them, and it depends on the company. It's one of those areas where it's tricky and there's a lot of judgment involved, so a lot of it just ends up not being on the balance sheet.

Intangible assets are non-physical assets that are expected to generate future economic benefits for the company. Under accounting rules, most internally generated intangibles are not recognized on the balance sheet, while acquired intangibles are recognized because they meet the relevant criteria. The key principle here is that recognition depends on whether the asset meets the definition and the recognition criteria, and internally generated intangibles generally fail to meet those criteria. The exception is acquired intangibles, which do appear on the balance sheet. So the treatment of intangibles comes down to the accounting framework and its recognition requirements, which is why most are excluded but some are included.

outcomes.term: How does CapEx & depreciation shift for mature vs new companies?

outcome.referenceAnswer: CapEx is cash spending on long-lived assets like plants and equipment; depreciation is the accounting charge that spreads the cost of past CapEx over those assets' useful lives. For a mature company, growth has slowed, so CapEx is low — mostly maintenance-level replacement spending. But depreciation is high, because the assets built during its expansion years are still on the books and still depreciating. A new or high-growth company is the mirror image: it is building out capacity, so CapEx is heavy, often a large share of revenue, while depreciation is low, because most of its assets are recent and haven't accumulated much depreciation yet. The mechanism connecting the two is a lag: today's depreciation reflects CapEx from years ago, so CapEx leads and depreciation trails it across the life cycle. That's why at a mature firm depreciation can actually exceed CapEx, while at a young firm CapEx far exceeds depreciation.

probes.text: CapEx and depreciation are both really important accounting concepts that investors look at closely. For a mature company, things tend to be a bit more stable, whereas a newer company is usually in a different phase of its life cycle. The relationship between the two can vary depending on the company and the industry it operates in. Generally speaking, there are some differences in how these items show up on the financial statements, and analysts often pay attention to them when comparing companies. It really depends on the specific situation, so you have to look at the context.

CapEx and depreciation are two key components of a company's financial statements that shift as the company evolves. For mature companies, they tend to be more stable and predictable over time, while for new companies, they can be more volatile and growth-oriented. This shift reflects the company's life cycle stage and its strategic priorities. Investors should analyze both metrics carefully to understand the company's capital intensity and future cash flow potential. It's important to consider these differences when comparing companies across different stages of maturity.
